orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, continuing her story to Lockwood. It is late summer 1801. Nelly has been locked in a room at Wuthering Heights for four days and five nights, while Cathy is held elsewhere in the house and Edgar lies dying at the Grange.

notes.n: To 'don' something is to put it on.

notes.g: A woman's hat that framed the face and tied under the chin.
A basket woven from willow twigs.
The housekeeper at Wuthering Heights, back from her trip.

notes.t: there is a talk about you
I never thought but you were sunk
notes.g: I was sure you had drowned.

notes.n: Moorland bogs could be deadly, especially in the dark or in fog.

notes.g: He had given you a room here.
Got stranded on a patch of dry ground in the marsh.

notes.n: 'Poorly' is everyday British English for unwell.

notes.g: He will be held to account for it.
I called out to Hareton Earnshaw.
notes.n: Zillah slips into dialect grammar here ('I calls', 'they's').

notes.tr: Oh, there have been strange goings-on, Mr. Hareton, since I went away. It's a sad shame about that fine young girl, and lively Nelly Dean.

notes.n: 'Queer' simply meant odd or strange.
'Likely' meant promising or good-looking.
A northern dialect word for someone cheerful and full of life.
In northern speech 'flit' means to move house.

notes.t: The bog-water got into her head
notes.g: The marsh water made her delirious (Heathcliff's lie).
Quite light-headed; not in her right mind.
I kept her where she was; I shut her in.
The funeral of the squire, Edgar Linton.
notes.n: The 'squire' was the leading landowner of a country district. Heathcliff speaks as if the funeral is already certain.
'Mistress' was a polite title for an older or married woman, the full form of 'Mrs.'
'Right' means 'very' here.

notes.g: The local doctor, who has looked after both families for years.
A long wooden bench with a high back, by the fire.

notes.m: Not someone renting: 'tenant' here just means occupant.

notes.g: Rock candy; a stick of hard sugar sweet.

notes.m: Not brainpower. 'Intelligence' meant news or information, as in 'military intelligence'.

notes.g: As if he had done nothing wrong.
notes.n: 'An innocent' could also mean a simpleton, which fits too.

notes.g: Make you cry out in pain.
So the marriage has taken place.
notes.n: Nelly does not tell us how Heathcliff arranged it, with Cathy under 21 and no consent from her father.

notes.g: So that she can get my inheritance.
notes.n: As Edgar's heir, Linton expects to inherit the Grange estate.
'Sung' was an accepted past-tense form then.

notes.t: she does not even know that you will have any
notes.g: Cathy doesn't even know you will inherit money.
notes.n: Cathy has never been told that the Grange estate will go to Linton rather than to her.
Still common in northern English: 'Give over!' means 'Stop it!'
The enclosed yard beside the house.

notes.t: master of the Grange after him
notes.g: The owner of Thrushcross Grange after Edgar.
notes.n: Linton is Edgar's heir: the estate passes to him, not to Cathy (Chapters XVI and XX).

notes.t: papa says everything she has is mine
notes.g: Heathcliff's claim, based on the marriage law of the time.
notes.n: Under English law, when a woman married, her money and personal belongings passed to her husband. This was called 'coverture'. So the cruel claim was largely true.

notes.t: two pictures in a gold case
notes.g: A locket holding two tiny portraits.
notes.n: Small painted portraits, called miniatures, were often worn on a chain as keepsakes.

notes.g: On the other side, my uncle (Edgar, her father).

notes.t: having my designs in encouraging his talk
notes.g: Having my own reasons for keeping him talking.
I shut my eyes; I blinked.
notes.m: Not a knowing wink. 'Wink' meant to close the eyes.

notes.g: I shut my eyes when I see.
notes.m: Not a knowing wink. 'Wink' meant to close the eyes.
An 'apartment' was a single room, not a flat.

notes.t: I bespoke the announcement of it myself
notes.g: I claimed the job of telling him myself.

notes.t: an image of sadness and resignation
notes.g: A picture of sorrow and calm acceptance.
Told him about our forced visit.
His sorrows, already too many to bear.
notes.n: A 'cup' of sorrow or suffering is an old, Bible-flavoured image.

notes.t: secure the personal property, as well as the estate, to his son
notes.g: Get Cathy's money and possessions, as well as the land, for Linton.
notes.n: The 'estate' is the land and house, which go to Linton as heir anyway. 'Personal property' means money and belongings, including the fortune Edgar saved for Cathy. Once she married, that passed to her husband.
Linton is a minor under his father's control. In Chapter XXI Heathcliff said that if Linton died, his property would go to his father.

notes.t: his will had better be altered
notes.g: He ought to change his will.
Hers outright, to use as she liked.
People appointed to hold and manage the money for her.
notes.n: In a trust, the trustees legally own the money but must use it only for the people named. Since Cathy would never own it outright, it could not pass to her husband, or through him to Heathcliff.

notes.t: for her use during life, and for her children
notes.g: She would have the benefit of it while she lived, and then her children would.

notes.t: it could not fall to Mr. Heathcliff should Linton die
notes.g: It could not end up with Heathcliff if Linton died.
notes.n: Otherwise anything Linton gained by marrying Cathy might pass to his father on Linton's death.
An 'attorney' was a lawyer who handled business such as wills and property. In England the title was later replaced by 'solicitor'.

notes.t: to demand my young lady of her jailor
notes.g: To demand that her jailer hand her over.
Edgar's lawyer, named here for the first time.
notes.n: In Chapter XVII, Edgar's lawyer had also been Hindley's.

notes.m: 'Suffer' here means allow, not feel pain.

notes.n: A 'bevy' is properly a flock of certain birds, such as quail.

notes.g: Actually attack it, like soldiers storming a castle.
The stone slabs at his front door.
The full moon nearest the start of autumn.
notes.n: It rises early and bright for several nights, helping farmers bring the harvest in late. So it is now around September.

notes.g: Threw her arms round my neck.

notes.t: chafing it into a faint colour
notes.g: Rubbing it until a little colour came back.
Nelly breaks off to speak to Lockwood directly.
To his wife, Cathy's mother, in heaven.

notes.m: 'Dinner' was the main meal, eaten in the middle of the day.

notes.t: He had sold himself to Mr. Heathcliff
notes.g: He had been bought by Heathcliff to work for him.
notes.n: So his delay was deliberate. Edgar died before he could change his will, and his plan to protect Cathy's money was never carried out.

notes.t: took upon himself to order everything
notes.g: Took it on himself to run everything.
Notice that they were dismissed and must leave.
notes.n: Servants were given 'notice', a warning period before they had to go.

notes.g: Power handed to him by someone else (Heathcliff).

notes.t: in the chapel, with his family
notes.g: Inside the church, under the Linton family monument.
notes.n: Catherine was buried outside, in a corner of the churchyard by the moor (Chapter XVI), and Edgar wished to lie beside her.

notes.t: There was the will, however, to hinder that
notes.g: But Edgar's will said where he was to be buried, and that stopped it.
notes.n: Wills often gave instructions for the funeral and burial.

notes.g: Now the wife of Linton Heathcliff.
notes.n: A married woman was formally called by her husband's full name, like 'Mrs. John Smith'. She is the young 'Mrs. Heathcliff' Lockwood met in Chapter II.

notes.m: 'Suffer' here means allow, not feel pain.

notes.t: her father’s corpse had quitted it
notes.g: Her father's body had left the house for burial.

notes.t: incur the risk of liberating her
notes.g: Take the risk of setting her free.

notes.t: conveyed up to the little parlour
notes.g: Carried up to the small sitting room.

notes.t: lest the dogs should raise an alarm
notes.g: For fear the dogs would bark and wake the house.
Coming upon her mother's old room.
notes.n: Probably the room where Lockwood slept in Chapter III, with a fir tree by its window.
A lattice window has small panes set in a crisscross of lead strips.
